'''''Artemisia''''' ({{IPAc-en|ˌ|ɑːr|t|ə|ˈ|m|iː|z|i|ə}} {{respell|art|ə|MEE|zee|ə}})<ref>{{cite book |title=Sunset Western Garden Book|date=1995|publisher=Leisure Arts|isbn=978-0-376-03851-7|edition=6th|pages=606–607}}</ref> is a large, diverse [[genus]] of plants belonging to the daisy family, [[Asteraceae]], with almost 500 species. Common names for various species in the genus include [[mugwort]], [[Artemisia absinthium|wormwood]], and [[sagebrush]].

Some [[Botanist|botanists]] split the genus into several genera, but DNA analysis<ref name="Watson_20022">{{cite journal |vauthors=Watson LE, Bates PL, Evans TM, Unwin MM, Estes JR|date=September 2002|title=Molecular phylogeny of Subtribe Artemisiinae (Asteraceae), including Artemisia and its allied and segregate genera|journal=BMC Evolutionary Biology|volume=2|article-number=17|doi=10.1186/1471-2148-2-17|pmc=130036|pmid=12350234|doi-access=free}}</ref> does not support the maintenance of the genera ''Crossostephium'', ''Filifolium'', ''Neopallasia'', ''Seriphidium'', and ''Sphaeromeria''; three other [[Segregate (taxonomy)|segregate]] genera—''Stilnolepis'', ''Elachanthemum'', and ''Kaschgaria''—are maintained by this evidence. Occasionally, some of the species are called sages, causing confusion with the ''[[Salvia]]'' sages in the family [[Lamiaceae]].

''Artemisia'' comprises [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]] [[herbaceous plants]] and [[Shrub|shrubs]], which are known for the powerful chemical constituents in their [[Essential oil|essential oils]]. ''Artemisia'' species grow in temperate climates of both hemispheres, usually in dry or semiarid habitats. Notable species include ''[[Artemisia vulgaris|A. vulgaris]]'' (common mugwort), ''[[Artemisia tridentata|A. tridentata]]'' (big sagebrush), ''[[Artemisia annua|A. annua]]'' (sagewort), ''[[Artemisia absinthium|A. absinthium]]'' (wormwood), ''A. dracunculus'' ([[tarragon]]), ''[[Artemisia abrotanum|A. abrotanum]]'' (southernwood), and [[Artemisia herba-alba|''A. herba-alba'']] (white wormwood). The [[leaves]] of many species are covered with white hairs.

Most species have strong aromas and bitter tastes from [[Terpenoid|terpenoids]] and [[Sesquiterpene lactone|sesquiterpene lactones]], which discourage [[herbivory]], and may have had a selective advantage.<ref name="fna2">{{cite web |year=2006|title=119. ''Artemisia'' Linnaeus|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=102682|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303200313/http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=102682|archive-date=2016-03-03|access-date=2009-07-06|work=[[Flora of North America]]}}</ref> The small flowers are [[wind-pollinated]].<ref name="fna2" /> ''Artemisia'' species are used as food plants by the [[Larva|larvae]] of a number of [[Lepidoptera]] species.

==Taxonomy==
The genus was erected by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753. The name ''Artemisia'' derives from the Greek goddess [[Artemis]] (Roman Diana), the namesake of Greek Queens Artemisia'' ''I and II.<ref>{{cite book |title=Shorter Oxford English Dictionary, 6th ed. |year=2007 |pages=3804 |publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0199206872|location=United Kingdom}}</ref> A more specific reference may be to [[Artemisia II of Caria]], a botanist and medical researcher (also a queen and naval commander), who died in 350 BC.<ref>{{cite web |title=Etymology|url=https://www.britannica.com/eb/article-9009683/Artemisia-II|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080507040945/http://www.britannica.com/eb/article-9009683/Artemisia-II|archive-date=2008-05-07|access-date=2012-06-07|website=Britannica.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Various|date=July 2014|title=Etymologia: Artemisinin|journal=Emerg Infect Dis|publisher=CDC|volume=20|issue=7|pages=1217|doi=10.3201/eid2007.ET2007|pmc=4073852}}</ref>

=== Classification ===
Classification of ''Artemisia'' is difficult.<ref name="fna2" /> Divisions of ''Artemisia'' prior to 2000 into subgenera or sections have not been backed up by molecular data,<ref name="Watson_20022" /> but much of the molecular data, as of 2006, are not especially strong.<ref name="fna2" /> The following identified groups do not include all the species in the genus.

====Subgenera ''Artemisia'' and ''Absinthium''====
Subgenera ''Artemisia'' and ''[[Absinthium]]'' are sometimes, but not always, considered the same. Subgenus ''Artemisia'' (originally ''Abrotanum'' Besser) is characterized by a heterogamous flower head with female outer florets and hermaphrodite central florets, and a fertile, glabrous receptacle. ''Absinthium'' DC, though sometimes merged with subgenus ''Artemisia'' is characterized by heterogamous flower head with female outer florets and hermaphrodite central florets, and a fertile, hairy receptacle. Generally, previously proposed monotypic and non-monophyletic subgenera have been merged with the subgenus ''Artemesia'' due to molecular evidence. For example, in 2011 using ribosomal DNA analysis of their own and a review of molecular data (such as ITS sequence analysis) of others, S. Garcia and colleagues argued that it was logical to rename several ''Sphaeromeria'' and ''Picrothamnus'' (formerly designated sister genera to ''Artemisia'') species as ''Artemisia'', as well as to revert some ''Sphaeromeria'' species back to ''Artemisia'', where they had been categorized previously.<ref name="Garcia_20112">{{cite journal |author1=Garcia S|author2=McArthur ED|author3=Pellicer J|author4=Sanderson SC|author5=Vallès J|author6=Garnatje T|display-authors=3|date=April 2011|title=A molecular phylogenetic approach to western North America endemic Artemisia and allies (Asteraceae): untangling the sagebrushes|journal=American Journal of Botany|volume=98|issue=4|pages=638–53|doi=10.3732/ajb.1000386|hdl=10261/50183|pmid=21613164|bibcode=2011AmJB...98..638G |hdl-access=free}}</ref> Part of this was due to research by Watson and colleagues, who found that the four subgenera were not monophyletic except for ''Dracunculus,'' after analyzing and matching the internal transcribed spacers of nuclear ribosomal DNA from many ''Seriphidium'' and ''Artemisia'' species, and the related genera ''Arctanthemum'' and ''Dendranthema''. The authors concluded that inflorescence morphology is not alone reliable for categorizing the genus or some subgenera, as qualities that previously demarcated them (such as homogamous, discoid, ray-less inflorescences) seemed to have undergone paralleled evolution up to seven times.<ref name="Watson_20022" /> ''Picrothamnus'' Nutt. ("bud sage"), now considered ''Artemisia spinescens'' and ''Sphaeromeria'' Nutt. ("chicken sage") are some examples, both endemic to North America.<ref name="Garcia_20112" />

==== ''Tridentatae'' ====
Section ''Tridentatae'' consists of eleven to thirteen species of coarse shrubs often known colloquially as "sagebrushes", which are very prominent parts of the flora in western North America.<ref name="kornkven2">{{cite journal |vauthors=Kornkven AB, Watson LE, Estes JR|date=December 1998|title=Phylogenetic analysis of Artemisia section Tridentatae (Asteraceae) based on sequences from the internal transcribed spacers (ITS) of nuclear ribosomal DNA|journal=American Journal of Botany|volume=85|issue=12|pages=1787–95|doi=10.2307/2446513|jstor=2446513|pmid=21680339 |bibcode=1998AmJB...85.1787K }}</ref> In some classifications, they have previously been considered part of the genus or subgenus ''Seriphidium'', although recent studies have contested this lineage to Old World species.<ref name="Watson_20022" /> ''Tridentatae'' was first articulated as a section by Rydberg in 1916, and it was not until McArthur et al. in 1981 that ''Tridentatae'' was elevated to a separate subgenus from ''Seriphidium''. The principal motive for their separation was geographical distribution, chemical makeup, and karyotype.<ref name="McArthur2">{{cite journal |vauthors=McArthur ED, Pope CL, Freeman DC|year=1981|title=Chromosomal Studies of Subgenus Tridentatae of Artemisia: Evidence for Autopolyploidy|journal=American Journal of Botany|volume=68|issue=5|pages=589–605|doi=10.2307/2442786|jstor=2442786}}</ref> Much of the debate surrounding Tridentatae is phytogeographic, thus habitat and geography are frequently cited when understanding the evolution of this endemic North American subgenus. Evolutionary cycles of wet and dry climates encouraged "diploid and polyploid races which are morphologically similar if not indistinguishable" (McArthur 598).

Autopolyploidy among plants is not uncommon, however ''Tridentatae'' exhibits a remarkable amount of chromosomal differences at the population level, rather than the taxon level. This contributes to the difficulty in determining ''Tridentatae's'' phylogeny. The subgenus' relative homogeneity within ploidies has enabled it to habitually hybridize and backcross, resulting in a high degree of genetic variation at the population level rather than the taxon level.<ref name="Garcia2">{{cite journal |author1=Garcia S|author2=Canela MA|author3=Garnatje T|author4=Mcarthur ED|author5=Pellicer J|author6=Sanderson SC|author7=Valles J|display-authors=3|year=2007|title=Evolutionary and ecological implications of genome size in the North American endemic sagebrushes and allies (Artemisia, Asteraceae)|journal=Biological Journal of the Linnean Society|volume=94|issue=3|pages=631–649|doi=10.1111/j.1095-8312.2008.01001.x|hdl=10261/28799|doi-access=free|hdl-access=free}}</ref> For instance, some articles suggest that to be monophyletic, section ''Tridentatae'' should exclude ''[[Artemisia bigelovii]]'' and ''[[Artemisia palmeri|A. palmeri]]''.<ref name="Watson_20022" /><ref name="kornkven2" /> and include ''A. pygmaea'' and ''A. rigida''.<ref name="Kornkven2">{{cite journal |vauthors=Kornkven AB, Watson LE, Estes JR|year=1999|title=Molecular Phylogeny of Artemisia Section Tridentatae (Asteraceae) Based on Chloroplast DNA Restriction Site Variation|journal=Systematic Botany|publisher=American Society of Plant Taxonomists|volume=24|issue=1|pages=69–84|doi=10.2307/2419387|jstor=2419387 |bibcode=1999SysBo..24...69K }}</ref> These results were supported by extensive chloroplast DNA (cpDNA) and nr[[DNA sequencing]] which departed from prior morphological, anatomical, and behavioral data.

Traditional lineages within ''Tridentatae'' were proposed on the basis of leaf morphology, habitat preference, and the ability to leaf-sprout, among other morphological and behavioral characteristics.<ref name="kornkven2" /> For instance, sagebrush in the ''A. tridentata'' lineage have tridentate leaves, live in especially arid habitats, and are unable to root-sprout.<ref name="kornkven2" /> This method of delimitation is problematic for species that do not fully adhere to the characteristics of a given lineage. The dry habitat and the presence of interxylary cork has often made the case for ''Tridentatae'' as a subgenus of its own,<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Moss EH|date=November 1940|title=Interxylary Cork in Artemisia with a Reference to ITS Taxonomic Significance|journal=American Journal of Botany|volume=27|issue=9|pages=762–68|doi=10.1002/j.1537-2197.1940.tb10947.x |bibcode=1940AmJB...27..762M }}</ref> and there is some ribosomal molecular evidence of a "''Tridentatae'' core" group for the subgenus.<ref>Shultz 2009, Garcia et al., 2011a</ref> In 2011, Garcia and colleagues proposed enlarging ''Tridentatae'' and organized it into the sections ''Tridentatae'', ''Nebulosae'', and ''Filifoliae'' based on previous research establishing relationships via ribosomal and nuclear DNA.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Garcia|first1=Sònia|last2=Garnatje|first2=Teresa|last3=McArthur|first3=E. Durant|last4=Pellicer|first4=Jaume|last5=Sanderson|first5=Stewart C.|last6=Vallès|first6=Joan|display-authors=3|name-list-style=vanc|date=August 2011|title=Taxonomic and Nomenclatural Rearrangements in Artemisia Subgen. Tridentatae, Including a Redefinition of Sphaeromeria (Asteraceae, Anthemideae)|journal=[[Western North American Naturalist]]|volume=71|issue=2|pages=158–63|doi=10.3398/064.071.0203|bibcode=2011WNAN...71..158G |issn=1527-0904|s2cid=84052786}}</ref><ref name="Garcia_20112" />

Intergrading forms are particularly common in recently radiated subgenera such as ''Tridentatae'', given their frequent reversals and [[convergent evolution]]. Global reviews of ''Artemisia'' using [[Internal transcribed spacer|ITS]] analysis support the hypothesis that ''Tridentatae'' has independent origins from Old World ''Seriphidium''<ref name="Watson_20022" /> These findings were compared with [[Pseudanthium|capitula]] morphology, challenging past assumptions based on floral characteristics. To better understand the rapid diversification and radiation relative to Old World ''Artemisia'', a closer study of Beriginian or Arctic species may provide missing links.<ref name="Riggins2">{{cite journal |vauthors=Riggins CW, Seigler DS|date=September 2012|title=The genus Artemisia (Asteraceae: Anthemideae) at a continental crossroads: molecular insights into migrations, disjunctions, and reticulations among Old and New World species from a Beringian perspective|journal=Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution|volume=64|issue=3|pages=471–90|doi=10.1016/j.ympev.2012.05.003|pmid=22580463 |bibcode=2012MolPE..64..471R }}</ref>

Section ''Nebulae'' includes ''[[Artemisia californica|A. californica]]'', ''[[Artemisia nesiotica|A. nesiotica]]'', and ''[[Artemisia filifolia|A. filifolia]]''.<ref name="Shultz2">{{cite journal |title=Revision of ''Artemisia'' subgenus ''Tridentatae'' |vauthors=Shultz LM|year=2009|journal=Systematic Botany Monographs|volume=89|pages=1–131}}</ref>

====''Seriphidium'' ====
The Old World species which different classifications put into the genus or subgenus ''Seriphidium'' consist of about 125 species native to Europe and temperate Asia, with the largest number of species in Central Asia.<ref name="pakistan2">{{cite web |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=5&taxon_id=130166 |title=22. ''Seriphidium'' (Besser ex Hook.) Fourr. |work=Flora of Pakistan |access-date=2006-05-01 |archive-date=2006-05-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060519201753/http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=5&taxon_id=130166 |url-status=live }}</ref> Some classifications, such as that of the [[Flora of North America]], exclude any New World plants from ''Seriphidium''.<ref name="fna2" /> They are [[Herbaceous plant|herbaceous plants]] or small shrubs.<ref name="pakistan2" />

''Seriphidium'' Besser was morphologically categorized by a homogamous flower head with all hermaphrodite florets and fertile and glabrous receptacle. ''Tridentatae'' was originally categorized as within ''Seriphidium'' due to floral, inflorescence, and leaf morphological similarities, until McArthur et al.'s analysis in 1981, which explained these similarities as convergent evolution.<ref>{{cite book |date=1986 |title=Proceedings : Symposium on the Biology of Artemisia and Chrysothamnus : Provo, Utah, July 9-13, 1984 / |doi=10.5962/bhl.title.109318 |last1=McArthur|first1=E. Durant|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/bibliography/109318|last2=Welch|first2=Bruce L.|publisher=Intermountain Research Station, Forest Service, U.S. Dept. of Agriculture|location=Ogden, Utah|access-date=2021-08-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221031161407/https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/bibliography/109318|archive-date=2022-10-31|url-status=live|name-list-style=vanc}}</ref> Old World ''Seriphidium'', with 125 species native to Europe and temperate Asia, was a previous classification of ''Seriphidium''. North American or "New World" ''Seriphidium'' and Old World ''Seriphidium''.{{clarify|date=April 2021}} North American ''Seriphidium'' were later placed into ''Tridentatae'' Rydb due to geographical distribution, growth habit, and karyotypic and chemotaxonomic similarities (such as presence of certain terpenols).<ref name="The Glacier Lakes Ecosystem Experim2">{{cite book |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/178208|title=The Glacier Lakes Ecosystem Experiments Site /|vauthors=Musselman RC|date=1994|publisher=US Dept. of Agriculture, Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Forest and Range Experiment Station|volume=249|location=Fort Collins, Colorado|doi=10.5962/bhl.title.99324|access-date=2021-08-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210201124004/https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/178208|archive-date=2021-02-01|url-status=live}}</ref>

==== Subgenus ''Dracunculus'' ====
One group which is well-supported by molecular data is subgenus ''Dracunculus''. It consists of 80 species found in both North America and Eurasia,<ref name="fna2" /> of which the best-known is perhaps ''[[Artemisia dracunculus]]'', the spice [[tarragon]].

''Dracunculus'' Besser. has historically been characterized morphologically by a heterogamous flower head with female outer florets and hermaphrodite central florets, but with a female-sterile, glabrous receptacle. ''Dracunculus'' is the most supported and resolved subgenus of ''Artemisia'', which includes ''Artemisia'' ''dracunculus'' L., known as the cooking spice tarragon. Chloroplast and ribosomal DNA sequence analysis in 2011 supported monophyly with two clades, one of which includes some North American endemic species as well as most species of Europe and Asia, while the second clade includes just ''A. salsoloides'' and ''A. tanaitica'', found in Eastern Europe and Siberia to the Western Himalayas.<ref name="Pellicer20112">{{cite journal |last1=Pellicer|first1=Jaume|last2=Vallès|first2=Joan|last3=Korobkov|first3=Aleksandr A.|last4=Garnatje|first4=Teresa|display-authors=3|name-list-style=vanc|date=2011|title=Phylogenetic relationships of Artemisia subg. Dracunculus (Asteraceae) based on ribosomal and chloroplast DNA sequences|journal=Taxon|volume=60|issue=3|pages=691–704|doi=10.1002/tax.603006 |bibcode=2011Taxon..60..691P }}</ref> This study places ''Dracunculus'' as one of the more recent subgenera within Artemisia, situating ''A. salisoides'' more basally on the tree, with North American endemic groups such as the sagebrushes having derived on the other end of a split from a common ancestor with ''Dracunculus''. Formerly proposed genera ''Mausolea'', ''Neopallasia'' and ''Turaniphytum'' are now argued to be within the subgenus ''Dracunculus'' due to ribosomal and chloroplast DNA evidence, with further species resolved as sister groups to ''Dracunculus'' due to phytochemical relationships.<ref name="Pellicer20112" /><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pellicer|first1=Jaume|last2=Hidalgo|first2=Oriane|last3=Garnatje|first3=Teresa|last4=Kondo|first4=Katsuhiko|last5=Vallès|first5=Joan|display-authors=3|name-list-style=vanc|date=2014|title=Life cycle versus systematic placement: phylogenetic and cytogenetic studies in annual Artemisia (Asteraceae, Anthemideae)|journal=Turkish Journal of Botany|volume=38|pages=1112–1122|doi=10.3906/bot-1404-102|hdl=10261/104027|doi-access=free|bibcode=2014TJBot..38.1112P |hdl-access=free}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
''Artemisia'' species are found on every continent except Antarctica,<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Vallès J|author2=Torrell M|author3=Garnatje T|author4=Garcia-Jacas N|author5=Vilatersana R|author6=Susanna A|display-authors=3|date=May 2003|title=The Genus Artemisia and its Allies: Phylogeny of the Subtribe Artemisiinae (Asteraceae, Anthemideae) Based on Nucleotide Sequences of Nuclear Ribosomal DNA Internal Transcribed Spacers (ITS)|journal=Plant Biology|volume=5|issue=3|pages=274–84|doi=10.1055/s-2003-40790|bibcode=2003PlBio...5..274V |hdl=10261/29191|issn=1435-8603|s2cid=260250772|hdl-access=free}}</ref> and have become part of many ecosystems around the world as a result. Below is currently a partial view of the importance of ''Artemisia'' species in ecosystems around the world.

===North America===
In North America, several species of ''Artemisia'' have become important parts of local environments, with wide adaptability. ''Artemisia papposa'' described by S.F.Blake & Arthur Cronquist can grow in the harsh, dry expanses of alkali flats, but also adapts to meadowlands.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Howell|first1=John Thomas|url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/46288|title=Leaflets of western botany.|last2=Eastwood|first2=Alice|date=1932–1966|publisher=J. T. Howell|volume=v.6 1950–1952|location=San Francisco|access-date=2019-12-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191219005451/https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/46288|archive-date=2019-12-19|url-status=live|name-list-style=vanc}}</ref>

Sagebrushes like ''A. papposa'' (of the ''Tridenteae'' subgenus) in general are found in the north and southwest areas of the North American continent. In the Intermountain West, in a habitat known as Sagebrush Steppe, ''A. tridentata'', ''A. tripartite'', and ''A. arbuscula'' grow alongside various grasses and species of bitter bush, creating an important environment for mule deer, pygmy rabbits, antelopes, and the sage grouse.<ref name="SSCP2">{{cite web |author=Idaho National Lab|title=Sagebrush Steppe Conservation Project|url=https://northamerica.wcs.org/wild-places/yellowstone-and-northern-rockies/sagebrush-steppe-habitat.aspx|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191219004011/https://northamerica.wcs.org/wild-places/yellowstone-and-northern-rockies/sagebrush-steppe-habitat.aspx|archive-date=2019-12-19|access-date=2019-12-18|publisher=Wildlife Conservation Society}}</ref> Understanding the phylogenetic relationships among the sagebrushes has been helpful in understanding the relationships among these plants and their environments, as well as learning more about how these plants formed these communities over long stretches of time.<ref name="Garcia_20112" /> Sagebrushes, which include ''A. ludoviciana'' and ''A. tridentata'' among others, can often also be found growing near junipers, particularly in the Elkhorn Mountain region, where the Juniper Woodlands form an ecosystem which provide cover for many animal species in both summer and winter months and storms. Because the habitat should burn only every 400–600 years,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kennard|first1=Deborah K.|last2=Moore|first2=Amanda J.|name-list-style=vanc|date=July 2013|title=Fire History, Woodland Structure, and Mortality in a Piñon-Juniper Woodland in the Colorado National Monument|journal=Natural Areas Journal|volume=33|issue=3|pages=296–306|doi=10.3375/043.033.0308|s2cid=86306521|doi-access=free}}</ref> with sagebrush shrubs living as long as 200 years (though potentially typically 88), this particular combination of ''Artemisia'' with other flora form an enduring habitat.<ref name="The Glacier Lakes Ecosystem Experim2" /> As it often goes, however, governments and farming businesses have often cleared sagebrush-juniper communities to create land for cow and domestic animal feedcrops, and Artemisia species may be declining due to this and invasive species such as cheatgrass.<ref name="Davies_20122">{{cite journal |author1=Davies GM|author2=Bakker JD|author3=Dettweiler-Robinson E|author4=Dunwiddie PW|author5=Hall SA|author6=Downs J|author7=Evans J|display-authors=3|date=July 2012|title=Trajectories of change in sagebrush steppe vegetation communities in relation to multiple wildfires|journal=Ecological Applications|volume=22|issue=5|pages=1562–77|doi=10.1890/10-2089.1|pmid=22908714 |bibcode=2012EcoAp..22.1562D }}</ref> Destabilization of the vegetation creates higher risk of fires, causing concern among the local conservation and wildlife groups.<ref name="SSCP2" /><ref name="Davies_20122" />

Due to their often extensive rhizome systems and other potential characteristics, however, some Artemisia species are often resilient to mowing or pulling, giving some species of Artemisia the ability to easily become invasive if introduced to comfortable, though non-native habitats.

* ''A. annua'' (native to Eurasia) is found in wetland habitats, and though it has been naturalized in much of North America it is considered weedy or invasive by some localities, such as Kentucky.<ref>{{cite web |title=Plants Profile for Artemisia annua (sweet sagewort)|url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=ARAN3|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190502234229/https://plants.usda.gov/core/profile?symbol=ARAN3|archive-date=2019-05-02|access-date=2019-12-18|website=plants.usda.gov|publisher=US Department of Agriculture}}</ref>
* This is particularly true of ''Artemisia vulgaris'', known as "common mugwort", in North America, where it was introduced by European colonists and settlers in the 1600s, when Jesuit priests and other colonizers may have first brought the herb for ointments and teas and likely also let into port cities via ballast dumping.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Barney|first=Jacob N.|name-list-style=vanc|date=June 2006|title=North American History of Two Invasive Plant Species: Phytogeographic Distribution, Dispersal Vectors, and Multiple Introductions|journal=Biological Invasions|volume=8|issue=4|pages=703–717|doi=10.1007/s10530-005-3174-9|bibcode=2006BiInv...8..703B |issn=1387-3547|s2cid=23543261}}</ref> A''rtemisia vulgaris'' will grow in dense groups and out-compete other plants in an area, in part due to its ability to grow on poorly enriched soils. Disturbed habitats, cities and roadsides or parking lots can easily become a field of ''A. vulgaris'', which is the Artemisia species designated as invasive by New York State.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Weston|first1=Leslie A.|last2=Barney|first2=Jacob N.|last3=DiTommaso|first3=Antonio|name-list-style=vanc|date=December 2005|title=A Review of the Biology and Ecology of Three Invasive Perennials in New York State: Japanese Knotweed (Polygonum cuspidatum), Mugwort (Artemisia vulgaris) and Pale Swallow-wort (Vincetoxicum rossicum)|journal=[[Plant and Soil]]|volume=277|issue=1–2|pages=53–69|doi=10.1007/s11104-005-3102-x|bibcode=2005PlSoi.277...53W |s2cid=25991516}}</ref>

== Cultivation and uses ==

=== Historical uses ===
Historically, ''Artemisia'' species were used in the attempted cure of various medical ailments, particularly related to women's health. In the [[Middle Ages]], ''Artemisia sp.'' were regarded as herbs of significant medical power, and described as "the most important master against all exhaustions".<ref name=":0">Szopa, Agnieszka, Joanna Pajor, Paweł Klin, Agnieszka Rzepiela, Hosam O. Elansary, Fahed A. Al-Mana, Mohamed A. Mattar, and Halina Ekiert. 2020. "''Artemisia absinthium'' L.—Importance in the History of Medicine, the Latest Advances in Phytochemistry and Therapeutical, Cosmetological and Culinary Uses" ''Plants'' 9, no. 9: 1063. <nowiki>https://doi.org/10.3390/plants9091063</nowiki></ref> By the Renaissance, ''Artemisia sp.'' (particularly ''A. absinthium'') was used particularly in the cure of digestive ailments, though the use of species such as ''A. vulgaris'' in women's health still persisted.<ref name=":0" />

==== Women's medicine ====
''Artemisia'' species (likely ''A. vulgaris'' and ''A. latifolia'') were described by the Greco-Roman physician [[Dioscorides]] (c. 40–90 AD) in his [[De materia medica]] as being used for "driving out the menstrual flow" and as an "abortifacient".<ref>Dioscorides, Pedanius (2000) [ca. 70]. Osbaldeston, Tess Anne (ed.). ''De materia medica: Being an herbal with many other medicinal matters. Written in Greek in the first century of the common era.'' Volume 2. Johannesburg: Ibidis. ISBN 0-620-23435-0. (from the Latin, after [[John Goodyer]] 1655])</ref> Historian John Scarborough (1940-2022) argued that Dioscorides' discussion of ''Artemisia'' ''sp.'' was an adaptation of folklore medicine that was commonly used in Asia Minor and Thrace.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Scarborough|first=John|date=2013|title=Adaptation of Folk Medicines in the Formal "Materia Medica" of Classical Antiquity|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24631899|journal=Pharmacy in History|volume=55|issue=2/3|pages=55–63|jstor=24631899 |pmid=25654901 |issn=0031-7047}}</ref> Learned medicine in the [[Middle Ages]] was largely based on [[Humorism|humoral theory]], which ascribed certain properties to herbs based on their use in heating/cooling and wetting/drying the body. ''A. vulgaris'' was described by the second century physician [[Galen]] (c. 129–216 AD) as having warming and drying effects, which recommended it to the treatment of urological diseases.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ekiert|first1=Halina|last2=Pajor|first2=Joanna|last3=Klin|first3=Paweł|last4=Rzepiela|first4=Agnieszka|last5=Ślesak|first5=Halina|last6=Szopa|first6=Agnieszka|date=2020-09-25|title=Significance of Artemisia Vulgaris L. (Common Mugwort) in the History of Medicine and Its Possible Contemporary Applications Substantiated by Phytochemical and Pharmacological Studies|journal=Molecules|language=en|volume=25|issue=19|page=4415 |doi=10.3390/molecules25194415|doi-access=free |pmid=32992959 |pmc=7583039 |issn=1420-3049}}</ref> The continued use of ''Artemisia'' as an abortifacient was described by twelfth-century women's health texts in the [[Trotula]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Riddle|first=John M.|title=Eve's herbs: a history of contraception and abortion in the West|date=1998|publisher=Harvard Univ. Press|isbn=978-0-674-27026-8|edition=2. print|location=Cambridge, Mass.}}</ref> This use was further integrated into university teaching by Johannes II Platearius (active 1120–1150) at the medical school of [[Salerno]], who proscribed a "wine of the decoction of artemisia" as a cure to blocked menstrual flow.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=van de Walle|first=Etienne|date=1997|title=Flowers and Fruits: Two Thousand Years of Menstrual Regulation|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/206401|journal=The Journal of Interdisciplinary History|volume=28|issue=2|pages=183–203|doi=10.2307/206401|jstor=206401 |issn=0022-1953|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
[[File:Gart_Artemisia_Text.jpg|thumb|Gart Artemisia Text]]
''Artemisia'' ''sp.'' continued to be used in women's health into the 16th century, and was described by [[Johann Wonnecke von Kaub]] in [[Gart der Gesundheit]] as the "mother herb", for use in "women's sickness". This continued in the English medical tradition as well, with mugwort (likely ''A. vulgaris'') being described as a "an herb appropriated to the female sex" for use in "bringing down the menses" by the English physician [[Nicholas Culpeper]]'s 1653 ''Complete Herbal.''<ref>{{Cite book |last=Culpeper|first=Nicholas|title=The Complete Herbal|orig-date=1653|date=2009|isbn=9781848373617|publisher=Arcturus}}</ref>

==== Historical medicinal uses ====
In Anglo-Saxon medicine, ''[[Artemisia vulgaris]]'' (mugwort) and ''A. pontica'' were described as treatments for soreness, pains and aches.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Van Arsdall |first=Anne |title=Medieval herbal remedies: the Old English Herbarium and Anglo-Saxon medicine |date=2010 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-88403-7 |edition=Digit. print. version |location=New York, NY London}}</ref>  ''A. vulgaris'' and ''A. absinthium'' were used to repel [[midges]] (Old English {{Lang|ang|mucgwyrt}} seems to be derived from ''mycg'' {{gloss|midge}}), [[Flea|fleas]] and [[Moth|moths]], intestinal worms, and in [[brewing]] (mugwort beer, mugwort wine) as a remedy against hangovers and nightmares.<ref name=":1" />

''[[Artemisia absinthium]]'' (known as wormwood or absinth) was used as a speculative [[Plague (disease)|plague]] cure during the [[Black Death]] as an antipyretic and antipasmodic, along with being reported to aid in wound healing.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fabbri |first=Christiane Nockels |date=2007 |title=Treating Medieval Plague: The Wonderful Virtues of Theriac |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/20617676 |journal=Early Science and Medicine |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=247–283 |doi=10.1163/157338207X205115 |jstor=20617676 |pmid=18175463 |issn=1383-7427}}</ref>

=== Modern uses ===
The aromatic leaves of some species are used for flavouring. Most species have an extremely bitter taste. ''[[Tarragon|A. dracunculus]]'' (tarragon) is widely used as a [[culinary herb]], particularly important in [[French cuisine]].

''[[Artemisia absinthium]]'' is used to make the highly potent spirit [[absinthe]]. [[Malört]] also contains wormwood. The aperitif [[vermouth]] is a wine flavored with aromatic herbs, but originally with wormwood.

''[[Artemisia arborescens]]'' (tree wormwood, or ''sheeba'' in [[Arabic language|Arabic]]) is an aromatic herb indigenous to the [[Middle East]] used in tea, usually with [[Mentha|mint]].

A few species are grown as [[Ornamental plant|ornamental plants]], the fine-textured ones used for clipped bordering. All grow best in free-draining sandy soil, unfertilized, and in full sun.

The largest collection of living Artemisia species, subspecies and cultivars is held in the National Collection of Artemisia in [[Sidmouth]], [[Devon]], [[United Kingdom|UK]], which holds about 400 taxa. The National Collection scheme is administered by Plant Heritage (formerly National Council for Conservation of Plants and Gardens, [[NCCPG]]) in the British Isles.<ref>{{cite web |title=Artemisia |url=https://www.plantheritage.org.uk/national-plant-collections/search-the-national-plant-collections/collection/1199/artemisia |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221030162911/https://www.plantheritage.org.uk/national-plant-collections/search-the-national-plant-collections/collection/1199/artemisia |archive-date=2022-10-30 |access-date=2022-10-30 |work=Plant Heritage Devon Group}}</ref>

=== Medicinal uses ===
[[Artemisinin]] (from ''[[Artemisia annua]]'') and derivatives are a group of compounds used to treat [[malaria]].<ref name="drugs2">{{cite web |date=21 March 2022 |title=Sweet wormwood (''Artemisia annua'' L.) |url=https://www.drugs.com/npp/sweet-wormwood.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231019180348/https://www.drugs.com/npp/sweet-wormwood.html |archive-date=19 October 2023 |access-date=7 August 2022 |publisher=Drugs.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=White NJ |date=July 1997 |title=Assessment of the pharmacodynamic properties of antimalarial drugs in vivo |journal=Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy |volume=41 |issue=7 |pages=1413–22 |doi=10.1128/AAC.41.7.1413 |pmc=163932 |pmid=9210658}}</ref> Treatments containing an artemisinin derivative ([[Antimalarial medication#Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs)|artemisinin-combination therapies]]) are now standard treatment worldwide for malaria caused by ''[[Plasmodium falciparum]]''.<ref name="drugs2" /> Administering ''Artemisia annua'' as dried whole leaves may cause resistance to develop more slowly than if it is administered as pure artemisinin.<ref name="Elfawal20152">{{cite journal |last1=Elfawal |first1=Mostafa A. |last2=Towler |first2=Melissa J. |last3=Reich |first3=Nicholas G. |last4=Weathers |first4=Pamela J. |last5=Rich |first5=Stephen M. |display-authors=3 |date=20 January 2015 |title=Dried whole-plant Artemisia annua slows evolution of malaria drug resistance and overcomes resistance to artemisinin |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=112,3 |issue=3 |pages=821–826 |bibcode=2015PNAS..112..821E |doi=10.1073/pnas.1413127112 |pmc=4311864 |pmid=25561559 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

[[Tu Youyou]] received the [[Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine|2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine]] for her discovery of the semisynthetic derivatives. She conducted research on traditional Chinese medicine and potential contributions to cures for malaria,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=White |first1=Nicholas J. |last2=Hien |first2=Tran T. |last3=Nosten |first3=François H. |date=December 2015 |title=A Brief History of Qinghaosu |journal=Trends in Parasitology |volume=31 |issue=12 |pages=607–610 |doi=10.1016/j.pt.2015.10.010 |issn=1471-4922 |pmc=4674626 |pmid=26776328}}</ref> on the basis of folk medicine and ancient Chinese texts.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tu Youyou {{!}} Biography, Malaria, Nobel Prize, & Facts {{!}} Britannica |url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Tu-Youyou |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231206231922/https://www.britannica.com/biography/Tu-Youyou |archive-date=2023-12-06 |access-date=2023-10-30 |website=www.britannica.com |language=en}}</ref> From reviewing ancient Chinese texts, they found that the compound artemisinin was optimally extracted at lower temperatures, as high temperature water poured over sweet wormwood leaves destroyed essential treatment properties.

The [[World Health Organization]] does not support the promotion or use of ''Artemisia'' plant material in any form for the prevention or treatment of malaria. They note that the plant form of medication has several problems. These include a lack of consistent artemisinin content, the content being low enough that recurrence of malaria often occurs, that the use of the plant may contribute to widespread artemisinin resistance, and that the plant form is not effective in malaria prevention.<ref>{{cite web |title=Effectiveness of Non-Pharmaceutical Forms of Artemisia annua L. against malaria |url=https://www.who.int/malaria/position_statement_herbal_remedy_artemisia_annua_l.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220212013437/https://www.who.int/malaria/position_statement_herbal_remedy_artemisia_annua_l.pdf |archive-date=12 February 2022 |access-date=30 April 2021 |website=World Health Organization International |publisher=World Health Organization}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=The use of non-pharmaceutical forms of Artemisia |url=https://www.who.int/news/item/10-10-2019-the-use-of-non-pharmaceutical-forms-of-artemisia |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210622143036/https://www.who.int/news/item/10-10-2019-the-use-of-non-pharmaceutical-forms-of-artemisia |archive-date=22 June 2021 |access-date=30 April 2021 |website=World Health Organization International |publisher=World Health Organization}}</ref>
